text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish newspaper publisher Marieberg is the latest company to announce it would move from the Stockholm Stock Exchange's main A list to the smaller O list because of a new wealth tax rule and more are expected to follow.
- All Swedish political parties are losing members except the Liberal Party and the Greens. The Centre Party has seen a steady decline under the leadership of Olof Johansson.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson continues to receive lower marks from among his party members than opposition party leader Carl Bildt.

- It will be more expensive for Swedes to travel abroad, especially in the United States and Britain, as the crown has weakened against currencies in 10 destinations that are typical for Swedish holidaymakers.
- The risk of telecoms group LM Ericsson moving its headquarters abroad has resulted in lower interest among newly graduated engineers to work for the group, a survey shows.

- Amersham Pharmacia Biotech, a new company formed through the merger of Pharmacia & Upjohn's life science unit with that of British health and technology group Amersham International, will become the world's largest supplier of biotech products.
- Some five billion crowns is needed to bail out ailing public housing firms which are owned by local governments. On average they have a negative debt-equity ratio of 72 percent.
- The National Debt Office says it may not need to borrow any more money this year, putting Swedish borrowing at its lowest level since the end of the 1980s.

- Sweden decided to finance a model farm project outside St Petersburg. The country's Baltic fund will contribute five million crowns to the project and dairy equipment company Alfa Laval Agri will invest the same.
- A two-month-long trial sale of factory outlet goods in a chain of cooperatively owned stores, KF, resulted in a 15 percent increase in total sales in one store. The project may be continued.

- The number of overnight stays in Sweden by British tourists rose 40 percent in the past three years to 440,000 in 1996. The Swedish tourist council in London says it has had twice as many enquiries so far this year compared to the first five months of 1996. Sweden is becoming more accessible to British travellers. Discount airline Ryanair, for example, is offering flights from London Standstead to Stockholm Skavsta from June 12 from 99 pounds sterling.
